title: Deep cerebral venous thrombosis mimicking influenza-associated acute necrotizing encephalopathy: a case report
case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman presented with headache and progressive alteration of consciousness. Five days earlier, she had developed fever and cough and tested positive for influenza B by nasal swab; she received a single inhalation of laninamivir. On admission she was stuporous (Glasgow Coma Scale E2V4M6) without focal neurologic deficits or meningeal signs. Laboratory tests showed iron-deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 7.8 g/dl, MCV 63.2 fl, iron 11 mg/dl), mild thrombocytosis (434×10^3/μl), an elevated D-dimer (3.9 μg/ml), and an IL-6 level of 43.9 pg/ml. Renal, hepatic and electrolyte panels were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) had an opening pressure of 300 mmH2O, xanthochromia with 1820 red cells/μl, protein 622.2 mg/dl, and 4 white cells/μl; cultures were negative, and PCR assays for herpes simplex virus, varicella–zoster virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus were all negative. Brain MRI revealed bilateral thalamic and caudate-nucleus lesions with left internal capsule involvement; on T2*-weighted images, there was diminished signal and enlargement of the deep cerebral veins.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute necrotizing encephalopathy was initially considered because “On the basis of the presence of bilateral thalamic lesions, a tentative diagnosis of ANE associated with influenza B infection was made…”  
2. Viral encephalitis was excluded as a cause given that “Polymerase chain reaction assays of CSF for herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, Epstein–Barr virus, and cytomegalovirus all had negative results.”  
3. Deep cerebral venous thrombosis was suspected when “observation of diminished signal and enlargement of deep cerebral veins on T2*-weighted MRI led us to reconsider the diagnosis of ANE.”  
4. CSF xanthochromia with a high red-cell count supported DCVT because “xanthochromia with a high red-cell count … has been reported in previous case reports of cerebral venous thrombosis but not in previous cases of ANE.”  
5. Elevated D-dimer further pointed toward DCVT, although it is “observable nonspecifically in a wide variety of frequently encountered conditions, such as dehydration or prolonged bed rest.”
